title: Pseudo-labeling and confirmation bias in deep semi-supervised learning
source: 2020 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN), 1-8
relevance: The canonical statement of the failure mode behind finding 4: a network trained on its own predictions overfits its early mistakes, and the mistakes are then reinforced rather than corrected, so the student converges toward the teacher's bias regardless of how much unlabeled data it sees. Explains why our coarse-year models inherit the 2020 mask's recall-by-height shape, and predicts that they should not be able to correct it from imagery alone. The mitigations it validates - mixup and a minimum labeled-data floor - translate for us into requiring some genuinely independent labels each year rather than relying entirely on projection from 2020.

title: The effects of different classification models on error propagation in land cover change detection
relevance: Quantifies how single-date classification error propagates into change detection and shows the propagation rate depends strongly on the classifier, with contextual (MRF) models propagating least and non-contextual models most. This matters because our whole product is a change series built from per-year masks: a fixed per-year recall deficit does not produce a fixed error in the temporal signal, and this paper gives the machinery to estimate what it does produce. Relevant to whether our per-crown validity intervals inherit a bias that grows or cancels over 18 acquisitions.

authors: Moraes, D., Campagnolo, M.L. & Caetano, M.
title: Training data in satellite image classification for land cover mapping: a review
relevance: Reviews where training labels come from - including labels inherited from earlier land-cover maps, which is precisely our 2020-mask-as-teacher setup - and collates what is known about how mislabeling degrades accuracy. Gives us the vocabulary and the citations to describe finding 4 as a recognized practice with recognized costs rather than an idiosyncratic shortcut. Also surveys correction strategies that stop short of full re-annotation, which is the constraint we are under.

title: Human-annotated label noise and their impact on ConvNets for remote sensing image scene classification
relevance: Measures real human label noise rather than synthetic flips and shows it is structured - concentrated in genuinely ambiguous classes - and therefore more damaging than the uniform noise most robustness methods assume. Directly applicable because our label noise is not random either: it is a systematic omission concentrated in the 5-15 m band, which is the worst case this paper identifies. Implies off-the-shelf noise-robust losses will not help us, because they assume the noise is not correlated with the feature we care about.

authors: Tang, Y., Zhang, G., Liu, J.K. & Qin, R.
title: Weakly supervised land-cover classification of high-resolution images with low-resolution labels through optimized label refinement
relevance: A correction strategy that fits our constraint exactly: refine coarse or mismatched labels automatically rather than re-annotating, and retrain - reported 2-14% average accuracy gain over training on the original labels. This is the methodological precedent for what we did in finding 5 with the NIR+CHM overlay, and it supplies the ablation design to show the refinement helped rather than just shifted the model toward one reference. Use it to structure the argument that our 0.68 to 0.87 recall gain is label correction and not label replacement with a different bias.
